title: Final Review and Exam Readiness
intro: Pulling the course together for exam day: the principles behind the best answers, the traps to avoid, how to pace 160 questions in three hours, and a high-yield review of all six domains, finishing with mixed practice questions.
objectives: Apply six cross-domain principles to choose the best answer in ISC2-style scenario questions
Recognise the most common traps, and pace the exam with checkpoints
Recall the highest-yield ideas from each of the six domains
Plan the final week, including both mock exams and targeted review

sections.title: The principles behind the best answers

blocks.title: Thinking like the exam, one last time

scenes.title: Thinking like the exam, one last time
scenes.sub: The principles behind the best answers, and exam-week strategy
scenes.say: You have covered six domains and thirty-seven modules. The exam won’t ask you to recite them; it will ask you to judge situations. A handful of principles sit behind almost every best answer. | This video draws those principles together, and covers how to use your final week and exam day.

scenes.title: Six principles behind the best answers

items.d: Ownership, policy and risk before tools
Tier first, then scale the controls

scenes.say: Six principles sit behind most best answers. | Govern first: establish ownership, policy and risk assessment before choosing tools. | People before systems: when safety or people’s rights are at stake, protecting them comes first. | Least privilege, always: for people, agents, pipelines and tokens alike. | Untrusted by default: treat inputs, retrieved content and model outputs as untrusted until checked. | Evidence over assurance: test, verify and record, rather than relying on claims, logos or a single passing test. | And proportionate to risk: tier the use case first, then scale the controls to match.

scenes.title: Tempting answer, best answer
rows: Ban it, or buy a product
Assess, tier, then enable with controls
Read its scope, verify, then contract
Fix the root cause; add regression tests
scenes.say: The same pattern appears in every domain: a tempting answer that acts too fast or trusts too much, and a best answer that follows the process. | In an incident, wiping and rebuilding destroys evidence. Contain first, preserve evidence, then eradicate. | Faced with a new AI tool, banning it drives use underground, and buying a product skips the thinking. Assess it, tier it, then enable it with controls. | With a vendor, a certificate logo proves little. Read its scope, verify the evidence, then contract for what is missing. | And with a test finding, blocking the reported input fixes nothing. Fix the root cause, and add regression tests.

scenes.title: Pacing 160 questions in three hours

events.d: Read each stem for its qualifier
On pace? Flag doubts and move on
Keep to about a minute each
Revisit flagged items if time allows

scenes.say: Pacing matters, because three hours for a hundred and sixty questions leaves little slack. | At the start, read each stem for its qualifier: best, most, first or least. | Aim to reach question forty at about forty-five minutes. If a question stalls you, choose your best answer, flag it and move on. | At question eighty, around the ninety-minute mark, take a breath and reset. | Keep to about a minute per question through question one hundred and twenty. | And aim to finish with a few minutes to spare, to revisit flagged items if time allows. Never leave a question unanswered.

items: Govern first; people before systems; least privilege
Untrusted by default; evidence over assurance; proportionate to risk
Prefer process over impulse: contain, assess, verify, fix causes
scenes.say: To recap. | Govern first, put people before systems, and apply least privilege everywhere. | Treat content as untrusted by default, prefer evidence over assurance, and keep controls proportionate to risk. | Choose process over impulse: contain, assess, verify, and fix root causes. | And pace yourself with checkpoints, answering every question.

blocks.md:
### Six principles, across the domains
| Principle | What it looks like in questions |
|---|---|
| **Govern first** | Inventory, ownership, policy and risk tiering come before tools or technical fixes (Domain 2) |
| **People before systems** | Protect people’s safety and rights first: stop harm, notify where required, keep humans able to intervene (Modules 2.6, 5.5) |
| **Least privilege, always** | Narrow tools and scopes for agents; no standing admin for people; short-lived tokens; separate duties (Modules 4.6, 4.7) |
| **Untrusted by default** | Inputs, retrieved documents, tool results and model outputs are checked, isolated or validated before they can act (Modules 4.4, 6.6) |
| **Evidence over assurance** | Read assurance reports’ scope; verify signatures and provenance; test repeatedly and record results (Modules 6.3, 6.4) |
| **Proportionate to risk** | Tier the use case, then match the depth of assessment, testing and oversight (Module 2.3) |

### Traps to recognise
- **The technically impressive answer** that skips governance, ownership or risk assessment.
- **The absolute answer:** ban all AI, block everything, guarantee zero risk.
- **The premature fix:** wiping, retraining or patching before containing and preserving evidence.
- **The trust shortcut:** a certificate, a vendor’s word, a signature or one passing test taken as proof.
- **The instruction-as-control answer:** "tell the model not to do it" in place of an enforced control outside the model.
- **The right action at the wrong time:** a good step that isn’t the FIRST step the question asks for.

### Your final week
| When | What |
|---|---|
| **Days 7 to 6** | Take Mock Exam 1 under exam conditions; review every miss by domain |
| **Days 5 to 4** | Revisit the weakest domains’ summaries, videos and knowledge checks; use smart practice |
| **Day 3** | Take Mock Exam 2; review misses, looking for patterns in the traps you fall for |
| **Day 2** | Light review: the four recap sections and exam callouts |
| **Day 1** | Rest. Confirm the test centre location, time and identification requirements |

On exam day, arrive early, read each stem and every option fully, look for the qualifier, eliminate clearly wrong options, and choose the answer that best fits the principles above.

blocks.title: The first step, again
blocks.md: A security manager learns that an internal AI agent, connected to the finance system, has made several unexpected payments overnight. The agent’s developer wants to retrain the model immediately, and the finance director wants the incident kept quiet until the cause is known.

q.q: What should the security manager do FIRST?
o: Retrain the model straight away, so the faulty behaviour is removed
Contain the agent and preserve evidence, then follow the incident plan
Keep the incident quiet for now, as the finance director has asked you to
Ask the agent itself to explain why it made the overnight payments
q.why: Containment with evidence preservation comes first: stop further payments, keep logs and traces, and follow the incident process, including legal and notification steps. Retraining destroys evidence and may not address the cause, secrecy can breach obligations, and a model’s self-explanation isn’t evidence.

q.q: Which answer pattern is MOST often a trap in ISC2-style AI security questions?
o: Establishing ownership and assessing risk before any controls are chosen
Telling the model in its prompt not to misbehave, instead of an enforced control
Containing an incident, and preserving evidence before eradication starts
Reading the scope of an assurance report before relying on its conclusions
q.why: Instructions to a model are guidance, not controls. Enforced controls outside the model, such as permissions, isolation and approvals, are what the best answers rely on.

scenes.title: Foundations and governance, revisited
scenes.say: Domain one, AI concepts, is ten per cent of the exam. Domain two, governance, ethics, risk and compliance, is seventeen per cent. Together they are more than a quarter of your score, and they underpin everything else. | This video revisits the ideas from both domains that questions return to most often.

scenes.title: Domain 1: AI concepts

items.d: Nested fields; all deployed AI is narrow

scenes.say: Domain one in six ideas. | AI contains machine learning, which contains deep learning, which contains generative AI. Every deployed system is narrow AI, however general it seems. | Supervised learning needs labels; unsupervised learning finds structure without them; reinforcement learning optimises actions for reward. Language models learn by self-supervised pre-training. | Transformers use attention over tokens, within a limited context window that holds instructions, history, retrieved documents and tool results together. | RAG adds retrieval at question time; agents add tools, memory and autonomy, and with them new attack surface. | Limitations matter for security: hallucination, drift and non-determinism. | And metrics: precision measures alert quality, recall measures threats caught, and the threshold is set by the cost of each kind of error.

scenes.title: Domain 2: governance, ethics, risk, compliance

items.d: EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001
Every AI use found, owned and tiered

scenes.say: Domain two in six ideas. | Laws bind, frameworks guide, and standards can be certified: the EU AI Act’s risk tiers and roles, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework’s govern, map, measure and manage, and the ISO/IEC 42001 management system. | Governance starts with an inventory: every AI use found, owned and risk-tiered, with clear roles across the three lines. | Responsible AI turns principles such as fairness, transparency and accountability into requirements, controls and evidence. | Risk management tiers use cases, records risks with owners, uses impact assessments such as DPIAs, and has residual risk formally accepted. | Privacy, intellectual property and third parties: lawful basis and minimisation, licences and provenance, and contracts that make your own compliance possible. | And oversight: clear human authority to intervene and stop, good records, and independent audit.

items: Know the AI family tree, paradigms, transformers, RAG and agents
Limitations and metrics drive security decisions
Laws, frameworks and standards: who must do what
Inventory, tiering, ownership, oversight and evidence
scenes.say: To recap. | Know the AI family tree, the learning paradigms, transformers, RAG and agents. | Remember that limitations and metrics drive security decisions. | Know which laws, frameworks and standards apply, and who must do what. | And build governance on an inventory, risk tiers, named owners, human oversight and evidence.

blocks.md:
### Domain 1: AI concepts and security fundamentals (10%)
| Topic | Remember |
|---|---|
| **AI landscape** | AI ⊃ ML ⊃ deep learning ⊃ generative AI; all deployed AI is narrow; AI is a supply chain of trust boundaries (Module 1.1) |
| **Paradigms** | Supervised (labels), unsupervised (structure), reinforcement (reward), self-supervised pre-training for LLMs |
| **Architectures** | CNNs for grids, RNNs for sequences, transformers with attention; hardware (GPUs, TPUs, memory) as attack surface |
| **GenAI** | Token-by-token generation; temperature and top-p; embeddings and vector search; context windows that mix instructions and data (Module 1.2) |
| **RAG and agents** | Retrieval adds untrusted content; agents add tools, memory and autonomy; permission-aware retrieval and least-privilege tools |
| **Limitations** | Hallucination, non-determinism, uncertainty, drift and model collapse; ground, verify and monitor (Module 1.3) |
| **Metrics** | Confusion matrix; precision versus recall; accuracy misleads on rare events; set thresholds by cost |

### Domain 2: governance, ethics, risk and compliance (17%)
| Topic | Remember |
|---|---|
| **Regulation and frameworks** | EU AI Act tiers (prohibited, high, limited, minimal, plus GPAI) and roles (provider, deployer); NIST AI RMF (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage); ISO/IEC 42001 certifiable management system (Module 2.1) |
| **Governance structures** | AI inventory, named owners, risk tiers, committee and CAIO, three lines model; policy → standard → procedure → guideline |
| **Responsible AI** | Principles → requirements → controls → evidence; fairness metrics conflict, so choosing one is a policy decision; transparency, explainability, interpretability (Module 2.2) |
| **Risk management** | Qualitative and quantitative methods (ALE = SLE × ARO); impact assessments (DPIA, FRIA); blast radius and autonomy; treat, then formally accept residual risk (Module 2.3) |
| **Privacy and IP** | Sensitive data hides in prompts, indexes, logs and weights; deletion from models is hard, so prevent; licences and copyright exceptions vary (Module 2.4) |
| **Third parties** | Due diligence by tier; contract for data use, notice, audit and exit; AIBOMs; shared responsibility (Module 2.5) |
| **Oversight and audit** | HITL approves before, HOTL supervises during; authority to intervene and stop; shadow AI discovery; documentation; internal and external audit (Module 2.6) |
| **Awareness** | Role-based training; measure behaviour, not completion; encourage reporting (Module 2.7) |

blocks.title: Which framework or concept?
pairs: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage
NIST AI Risk Management Framework
A certifiable AI management system with Annex A controls
ISO/IEC 42001
Prohibited, high, limited and minimal risk tiers
EU AI Act
Share of real threats that an alert rule actually catches
Recall
A person approves each decision before it takes effect
Human in the loop (HITL)

q.q: A business unit is already using several unapproved AI tools. What should the AI governance lead do FIRST?
o: Block every AI tool at the network level until a full policy is written
Discover and inventory the AI use, then assess and tier each one
Buy an enterprise AI platform and require everyone to switch to it
Ask the business unit to stop using AI until next year’s budget
q.why: Governance starts with visibility: discover and inventory the AI use, then assess, tier and decide. Blanket bans drive use underground, and buying a platform skips the assessment.

scenes.title: Data, models and architecture, revisited
scenes.say: Domain three, data management, privacy and model security, is nineteen per cent of the exam. Domain four, secure architecture, engineering and identity, is eighteen per cent. Together they are more than a third of your score. | This video revisits the ideas from both domains that questions return to most often.

scenes.title: Domain 3: data and model security

items.d: At rest, in transit, in use; keys

scenes.say: Domain three in six ideas. | Data governance: owners, stewards and custodians; classification that survives chunking and embedding; and provenance, lineage and custody records. | Privacy controls: purpose and lawful basis first, then minimisation, masking and tokenisation. Pseudonymised data is still personal data, anonymisation must be proven, and differential privacy trades accuracy for a provable limit. | Training data integrity: version datasets by hash, validate them, and layer defences against poisoning, which can need surprisingly few samples. | Cryptography: protect data at rest, in transit and in use, with well-governed keys, and trusted execution environments where needed. | Model governance: named owners, independent validation, model cards, an approved registry, and deployment gates that accept only signed, approved versions. | And model protection: limit outputs and queries against extraction, sign and verify model files, and verify everything that comes through the supply chain.

scenes.title: Domain 4: architecture, engineering and IAM

items.d: Zero Trust, defence in depth, threat models
Before, around and after the model

scenes.say: Domain four in six ideas. | Secure design: Zero Trust, defence in depth, secure defaults and threat modelling at every trust boundary, with architecture decisions recorded. | Infrastructure: hardened notebooks and platforms, isolated training enclaves, sandboxed agent code, and quotas that stop runaway consumption. | Pipelines: ephemeral runners, pinned inputs, signed provenance, gated promotion, and lineage captured automatically. | Guardrails sit before, around and after the model, but the harness, not the model, enforces safety, and no guardrail stops every injection. | Identity: users, privileged humans, workloads, agents and tools all need unique identities, with delegation rather than impersonation. | And authorisation: narrow tools, least privilege, just-in-time access, scoped short-lived tokens, and policy enforced outside the model.

items: Own, classify and trace data; minimise and protect it
Version and validate training data; govern and sign models
Design with Zero Trust; gate pipelines; enforce in the harness
Identify every identity; least privilege, enforced outside the model
scenes.say: To recap. | Own, classify and trace data, and minimise and protect it. | Version and validate training data, and govern, sign and verify models. | Design with Zero Trust, gate pipelines, and enforce safety in the harness. | And give every human and non-human identity least privilege, enforced outside the model.

blocks.md:
### Domain 3: data management, privacy and model security (19%)
| Topic | Remember |
|---|---|
| **Data governance** | Owner accountable, steward manages, custodian operates; controller and processor roles; sovereignty, residency and localisation; provenance, lineage and custody (Module 3.1) |
| **Privacy controls** | Privacy by design; lawful basis; minimisation; masking and tokenisation; pseudonymised ≠ anonymous; differential privacy (ε); GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS duties (Module 3.2) |
| **Training data** | Version by content hash; availability, targeted and backdoor poisoning; memorisation, extraction and membership inference; label integrity (Module 3.3) |
| **Data protection** | DSPM, CSPM and DLP; encryption at rest, in transit and in use; envelope encryption and key ownership (BYOK, HYOK); crypto-agility (Module 3.4) |
| **Model governance** | Named owners; independent validation; model and system cards; approved registry; signed artefacts; staged release with rollback (Module 3.5) |
| **Model CIA** | Protect weights and prompts; limit outputs and queries against extraction; watermarks and fingerprints as evidence; hash, sign and verify at deploy and load (Module 3.6) |
| **Supply chain** | Know every source; pin by hash and mirror; verify provenance and authenticity; re-test fine-tunes for safety (Module 3.7) |

### Domain 4: secure architecture, engineering and IAM (18%)
| Topic | Remember |
|---|---|
| **Secure design** | Zero Trust; defence in depth across identity, input, output and action layers; threat modelling at trust boundaries; architecture decision records (Module 4.1) |
| **Infrastructure** | Harden ML tooling; training enclaves without egress; sandboxed agent code; tenant isolation; quotas and rate limits (Module 4.2) |
| **Pipelines** | Ephemeral runners; pinned inputs; signed provenance (SLSA); quarantine, curate and snapshot data; automatic lineage; gates (Module 4.3) |
| **Guardrails** | Before, around and after the model; separate instructions from untrusted content; measure filter error rates; harness patterns such as plan-then-execute (Module 4.4) |
| **Identity** | Human and non-human identities; workload identity federation; delegation with user and agent in tokens; SSO with SAML or OIDC (Module 4.5) |
| **Authorisation** | Narrow tools; RBAC, ABAC and PBAC; just-in-time access; scoped tokens; excessive agency and over-delegation (Module 4.6) |
| **Lifecycle and auditing** | Identity inventory including agents; joiner, mover, leaver; access reviews; identity posture management; per-identity metering (Module 4.7) |

blocks.title: Which control fits?
pairs: Prove which dataset version trained a model
Content-hashed dataset versions and lineage
Stop a model file being swapped before deployment
Signature and digest checks at the deployment gate
Limit what an agent can do if it is manipulated
Narrow, least-privilege tools enforced outside the model
Give an engineer production access only when needed
Just-in-time access, approved and auto-revoked
Keep personal data out of a training set
Minimisation, masking or tokenisation before training

q.q: An agent’s system prompt tells it never to share customer data, yet testing shows it can be manipulated into doing so through retrieved documents. Which control BEST addresses this?
o: A stronger warning in the system prompt, repeated several times for emphasis
Permission-aware retrieval and output DLP, enforced outside the model
Training staff to avoid uploading documents that contain hidden text
Switching to a model that scores higher on public safety benchmarks
q.why: Controls enforced outside the model, such as retrieval that respects permissions and output data loss prevention, limit what manipulation can achieve. Prompts, staff awareness and benchmarks don’t enforce anything.

scenes.title: Operations, threats and testing, revisited
scenes.say: Domain five, secure AI operations and incident response, is nineteen per cent of the exam. Domain six, AI threats, testing and lifecycle management, is seventeen per cent. They test whether you can run AI securely day to day, and find and fix its weaknesses. | This video revisits the ideas from both domains that questions return to most often.

scenes.title: Domain 5: operations and incident response

items.d: Prompts, retrieval, tools, one trace ID

scenes.say: Domain five in six ideas. | Readiness: named roles in a RACI, playbooks and runbooks, pre-agreed authority to stop a model, and release criteria that include monitoring and rollback. | Telemetry: prompts, outputs, retrieval, tool calls and guardrail decisions, joined by one trace ID, with sensitive content masked at collection and logs protected from tampering. | Detection across inputs, retrieved content, outputs, agent behaviour and cost, combining rules, classifiers and baselines. | Vulnerability management: a register covering models, data and agents, prioritised by exposure and consequence rather than base scores alone. | Containment climbs a ladder, from tighter guardrails through throttling, restriction, isolation and rollback to taking a system offline, preserving evidence throughout. | And recovery: restore only verified clean versions, meet recovery objectives, and run blameless post-incident reviews that update playbooks and the threat register.

scenes.title: Domain 6: threats, testing and lifecycle
scenes.say: Domain six in six ideas. | Threat modelling: STRIDE for categories, PASTA for risk, MAESTRO for agentic layers, drawing threats from MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP lists. | Secure lifecycle: security gates in MLOps and LLMOps pipelines, every behaviour-changing component versioned in a release manifest, and staged rollouts with tested rollback. | Supply chain: read assurance evidence critically, check licences along the pedigree, verify provenance with hashes and signatures, and maintain AI bills of materials. | Testing: scope the whole system under rules of engagement, test every entry point safely, repeat tests and report success rates, and combine human red teaming with automation. | Findings: triage by severity, exploitability, reproducibility and impact; separate vulnerabilities from model limitations; map to frameworks; and communicate for each audience. | And mitigations: target root causes, prioritise by risk and feasibility, validate with regression tests, and monitor residual risk.

items: Prepare roles and runbooks; collect joined, protected telemetry
Contain first, preserve evidence, recover to clean versions
Model threats, gate the lifecycle, verify the supply chain
Test safely and repeatedly; fix root causes; watch residual risk
scenes.say: To recap. | Prepare roles and runbooks, and collect joined, protected telemetry. | In incidents, contain first, preserve evidence, and recover only to verified clean versions. | Model threats, gate the lifecycle, and verify the supply chain. | And test safely and repeatedly, fix root causes, and keep watching the residual risk.

blocks.md:
### Domain 5: secure AI operations and incident response (19%)
| Topic | Remember |
|---|---|
| **Readiness** | No standing production access; RACI with named deputies; pre-agreed authority to stop a model; playbooks decide, runbooks execute (Module 5.1) |
| **Telemetry** | Collect prompts, outputs, retrieval, tool calls and guardrail decisions; one trace ID; mask at collection; protect log integrity (Module 5.2) |
| **Detection** | Scan retrieved content, not just prompts; baseline agents; treat cost anomalies as security signals; verify model and data integrity at runtime (Module 5.3) |
| **Vulnerabilities** | Register model, data, configuration, supply chain and agent weaknesses; prioritise with context (CVSS, EPSS, KEV, SSVC); AIBOM matching (Module 5.4) |
| **Response** | Classify (injection, jailbreak, poisoning, theft, leakage, agent misuse); severity; legal early for notification clocks; containment ladder; suspend pipelines; terminate agents safely (Module 5.5) |
| **Investigation** | AI kill chains mapped to ATLAS; one UTC timeline; root causes; attribution with stated confidence; eradicate across data, models, indexes and memory (Module 5.6) |
| **Recovery** | Roll back, restore or rebuild to verified versions; RTO and RPO; circuit breakers and kill switches; blameless reviews; secure decommissioning (Module 5.7) |

### Domain 6: AI threats, testing and lifecycle management (17%)
| Topic | Remember |
|---|---|
| **Threat modelling** | STRIDE, PASTA, MAESTRO; actors including insiders and non-human actors; adversarial ML attacks; GenAI, RAG and agent threats; availability and cost attacks (Module 6.1) |
| **Lifecycle and change** | Security at every stage; environment separation; everything that changes behaviour is a change; release manifests; canaries and rollback of the whole bundle (Module 6.2) |
| **Supply chain** | Read SOC 2 scope, exceptions and CUECs; data ownership and licences along the pedigree; hashes, signatures and attestations; AIBOMs with VEX (Module 6.3) |
| **Testing** | Scope, objectives, scenarios and rules of engagement; canaries; attack success rates; red teaming cycle and frameworks; AI-assisted tools with calibrated judges (Module 6.4) |
| **Findings** | Triage factors; vulnerability versus limitation; ATLAS, OWASP and CWE mapping; reproduction packages; audience-specific reporting (Module 6.5) |
| **Mitigations** | Targeted controls and injection-resistant design patterns; filtering, sandboxing, rate limiting, watermarking; prioritisation with interim controls; regression gates; residual risk monitoring (Module 6.6) |

blocks.title: Which step comes first?
pairs: An agent is making unexpected changes in production
Contain it, preserving evidence
A new AI feature is proposed for a high-risk use
Threat model and tier it
A red team finding has been fixed
Retest with variants before closing
A provider announces a model retirement
Raise a change and evaluate the replacement
A public dataset you used is reported as poisoned
Query AIBOMs and lineage to find affected models

q.q: Testing shows a fix reduced attack success from 30% to 2%. The team wants to close the finding. What should ALSO be confirmed?
o: That the original tester personally agrees with the team’s choice of fix
That utility holds, variants fail, and the cases join a regression gate
That the model vendor has published a public statement about the attack
That the finding has been open for at least a full quarter of the year
q.why: Validation needs held-out variants, preserved utility and ongoing regression protection, so the fix generalises and stays effective.

quiz.q: About how long can you spend on each question if you want to finish the pilot exam on time?
o: About 30 seconds, since most questions are simple recall
About 67 seconds each, for 160 questions in three hours
About two minutes, with review time added at the end
About five minutes, as the exam has only 40 questions
quiz.why: 180 minutes for 160 questions is about 67 seconds each, so pacing checkpoints matter.

quiz.q: Why is "instruct the model not to do it" rarely the best answer?
o: Prompts are far too expensive to maintain at any real scale of use
Instructions guide a model; enforced controls outside it stop harm
Regulators prohibit the use of system prompts in production
Models ignore every instruction written in their system prompt
quiz.why: A prompt is guidance the model may not follow under manipulation; permissions, isolation and approvals are enforced regardless.

quiz.q: A question asks what to do FIRST after discovering an AI security incident. Which answer is usually best?
o: Rebuild the affected system immediately from scratch
Contain the incident, and preserve the evidence
Publish a full statement to all customers at once
Retrain the model on fresh data straight away
quiz.why: Containment with evidence preservation comes first; rebuilding or retraining early destroys evidence and may miss the cause.

quiz.q: Which NIST AI RMF function covers culture, policies and accountability?
o: Map, which sets the context and identifies risks
Govern, which is cross-cutting across the others
Measure, which analyses and tracks identified risks
Manage, which prioritises and treats the risks
quiz.why: Govern is the cross-cutting function covering culture, policies, roles and accountability.

quiz.q: Why can accuracy mislead when evaluating a detector for rare attacks?
o: Accuracy can only be calculated for image classification models
A detector that flags nothing can still score very highly
Accuracy always overstates recall by exactly a factor of two
Rare attacks can never be included in evaluation datasets
quiz.why: When attacks are rare, predicting "benign" every time gives high accuracy and zero recall.

quiz.q: Under the EU AI Act, who carries most obligations for a high-risk AI system?
o: The end users who interact with the system each day
The provider who places the system on the market
The cloud company that hosts the underlying model
The national standards body in each member state
quiz.why: Providers carry most duties, such as conformity assessment and technical documentation; deployers have their own, narrower duties.

quiz.q: Why should training datasets be versioned by content hash?
o: Hashes compress datasets, so training runs much faster
To prove exactly which data trained a model, and roll back
Regulators require hashes for every spreadsheet in use
Hashing removes personal data from datasets automatically
quiz.why: Content hashes tie each model to the exact data it used, supporting investigations, rollback and integrity checks.

quiz.q: What does just-in-time access provide for AI platform administrators?
o: Permanent administrator rights, for faster troubleshooting
Time-limited, approved access that is revoked automatically
Shared administrator accounts for everyone in the team
Access granted only to models and never to any people
quiz.why: Just-in-time access removes standing privilege: access is requested, approved, scoped, recorded and revoked automatically.

quiz.q: Which step on the AI containment ladder is LEAST disruptive?
o: Taking the whole AI system offline until further notice
Tightening guardrails and filters around the system
Rolling back the system to an earlier model version
Isolating the system completely from the network
quiz.why: The ladder climbs from tighter guardrails, through throttling, restriction, isolation and rollback, to taking the system offline.

quiz.q: Which threat modelling method is designed around the layers of agentic AI systems?
o: STRIDE, which classifies threats into six categories
MAESTRO, which models threats layer by layer for agents
PASTA, which is a seven-stage risk-centric process
DREAD, which scores threats by damage and exploitability
quiz.why: MAESTRO structures threat modelling across the layers of agentic AI systems, including cross-layer threats.

quiz.q: Why are AI security test results reported as success rates over repeated attempts?
o: Rates are required by every AI regulation now in force
Outputs vary, so a single attempt can prove very little
Repeated attempts make the model more secure over time
Rates hide the attack details from people reading reports
quiz.why: The same input can succeed on one attempt and fail on another, so a rate over many attempts is the meaningful measure.

quiz.q: What is an AI bill of materials MAINLY used for?
o: Setting the price of AI services for different customers
Finding affected systems fast when a component is compromised
Replacing the model card that documents each model in use
Training models faster on newly purchased GPU hardware
quiz.why: An AIBOM records models, data, software and hardware dependencies, so advisories can be matched to affected systems quickly.

exam.q: A hospital deploys an AI triage assistant. Clinicians accept its recommendations 99% of the time, including when it is wrong. Which concern does this MOST indicate?
o: The model’s accuracy is too high for it to be used in clinical settings
Automation bias is undermining effective human oversight of the system
The hospital has too many clinicians reviewing the assistant’s outputs
The assistant needs a larger context window to give better answers
exam.why: Near-total acceptance, even of wrong outputs, indicates automation bias: oversight exists on paper but isn’t effective. Training, interface design and monitoring of override rates help.

exam.q: A company wants to fine-tune a model on customer support transcripts that contain personal data. Which step should come FIRST?
o: Start fine-tuning now, and anonymise the data afterwards if anyone asks
Confirm the purpose and lawful basis, and complete a DPIA first
Buy a larger GPU cluster to speed up the fine-tuning process
Publish the transcripts, so customers can review what is used
exam.why: Purpose, lawful basis and a data protection impact assessment come before processing, and determine minimisation and other safeguards.

exam.q: An internal audit finds several AI models in production with no named owner and no risk tier. What is the BEST corrective action?
o: Decommission every model without a named owner immediately
Assign owners, tier each model, and record both in the inventory
Ask each model’s vendor to take full ownership of its model
Wait for the next audit, to see whether the problem persists
exam.why: Accountability and risk-based control depend on named owners and tiers recorded in the inventory. Decommissioning everything is disproportionate, and vendors can’t own your risk.

exam.q: A model registry accepts uploads from any engineer, and deployments pull the "latest" version. Which change MOST improves integrity?
o: Allow only senior engineers to upload models to the registry
Pipeline-only writes, signed versions, and deployment by digest
Back up the registry every night to a second cloud region
Rename the models clearly, so engineers always pick the right one
exam.why: Restricting writes to the pipeline, signing versions and deploying by immutable digest stop tampering and substitution. Seniority, backups and naming don’t.

exam.q: An agent uses one long-lived API key with full CRM access for every task. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Rotate the key once a year, and keep its full set of permissions
Per-task, scoped, short-lived tokens issued through a broker
Put the key in the system prompt, so the model can use it
Share the key with the support team, so they can audit its use
exam.why: Scoped, short-lived, per-task credentials limit what a manipulated agent can do. Annual rotation keeps excessive privilege, and keys in prompts or shared are exposed.

exam.q: Researchers can reconstruct parts of a model’s training data by querying its API. Which combination BEST reduces this risk?
o: Publishing the training data, so reconstruction no longer matters
Deduplicating training data, limiting outputs, and monitoring queries
Increasing the model’s temperature setting for every single response
Moving the API to a new, unpublished domain that is harder to find
exam.why: Duplication drives memorisation, while output limits, rate limits and monitoring raise the cost of extraction. Publishing, temperature changes and obscurity don’t address the cause.

exam.q: A SOC sees a spike in tool calls from one agent to an external file-sharing service. What should happen FIRST?
o: Delete the agent and all its logs, to stop the activity at once
Contain: pause or restrict the agent, and preserve the traces
Email the file-sharing service and ask it to investigate
Wait to see whether the activity stops on its own
exam.why: Containment that preserves evidence stops possible exfiltration and keeps the traces needed for investigation.

exam.q: After a poisoning incident, a team plans to "unlearn" the poisoned samples instead of retraining. What is the BEST advice?
o: Unlearning is always preferable, because it is faster and cheaper
Prefer retraining on clean data, or restoring a verified checkpoint
Keep the model unchanged, because poisoning effects fade over time
Add a warning to all outputs, and continue operating as normal
exam.why: Machine unlearning offers weaker guarantees. Retraining on cleaned, verified data, or restoring a verified clean checkpoint, gives stronger assurance.

exam.q: A vendor’s SOC 2 Type II report carves out the model provider the vendor depends on. What should the assessor do?
o: Accept the report, since carved-out suppliers are covered by it anyway
Obtain assurance for the model provider, or agree compensating terms
Reject the vendor, since carve-outs always show a dishonest supplier
Ask the vendor to delete the carve-out section from its report
exam.why: Carved-out suppliers aren’t covered, so separate evidence or compensating contractual and technical controls are needed.

exam.q: A red team reports that indirect injection makes an agent send data externally in 4% of attempts. Leadership asks whether 4% is low enough to ignore. What is the BEST answer?
o: Yes, since any rate under 5% is considered acceptable by default
No: at scale it will happen often, and the impact is a data breach
Yes, because the red team could only make it work occasionally
No, but only because regulators ban any non-zero failure rate
exam.why: Low rates are frequent at scale, and the impact is severe, so the finding needs mitigation. Acceptance must be based on risk, not on an arbitrary threshold.

exam.q: Which response is MOST likely to be correct when a question asks how to manage employees using unapproved AI tools?
o: Block every AI website permanently at the corporate firewall
Discover the use, assess it, and offer approved alternatives
Discipline every employee who is found using the tools
Ignore it, since personal productivity tools are low risk
exam.why: Shadow AI is managed by discovering and assessing use, then enabling safe, approved options. Blanket bans and punishment drive use underground.

exam.q: A model provider updates its model, and scheduled tests show attack success rising above the agreed threshold. What should happen?
o: Nothing, until the next annual review of the accepted risks
Treat it as a breached KRI: reassess, mitigate and gate releases
Switch off the monitoring until the provider fixes its model
Raise the threshold, so that the latest result passes again
exam.why: A breached key risk indicator triggers reassessment and treatment, with release gates preventing further exposure.
